q1: The first merges rebuild frequent two-byte Urdu letters (for example merges 1, 2, 4 and 6 to 9), followed by space+letter pieces and common endings. Merges 3, 5, 12 and 37 are not valid UTF-8 on their own because they are a lead byte (D8 or D9), sometimes joined with the leading space or a letter, so BPE merges by byte frequency and not by character boundaries. The first whole word is merge 30, the word ␣کی, and the first 3+ letter word is merge 40, ␣میں; the 20 longest tokens are mostly long Pakistani news compounds, plus junk such as a run of 16 full stops and a line of dashes that the cleaning missed.
q2: On test.txt my tokenizer needs 1.121 tokens per word, compared with 5.824 for GPT-2 and 1.531 for o200k_base, because my merges were learned from Urdu text. It is worse than both on roman_urdu (2.789 vs 2.0 and 1.421) and worse than o200k on urdu_with_english (1.667 vs 1.278), since Latin-script text is rare in my corpus. These numbers favour my tokenizer, because test.txt comes from the same kind of data it was trained on, o200k has a 200k vocabulary against my 50k, and the hand-picked inputs are only 14 to 29 words each.
q3: roman_urdu (2.789 tokens per word, against 1.121 on test.txt): the corpus is almost entirely Urdu script, so Latin letters have few merges and split into short pieces. unnormalised_variants (3.5 tokens per word): Arabic yeh, kaf and heh and tatweel are different byte sequences from the normalised letters, so the same words fragment unless normalize() is applied first. long_digit_strings (8.0 tokens per word): a long number counts as one word and digits only merge into short runs, so it needs many tokens; GPT-2 (7.333) and o200k (6.667) also need many, so this is hard for all three.
